evidence: Cic. Clu. 123: quae cum ita sint (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Off. 1.54: quī cum ūnā domō jam capī nōn possint, in aliās domōs … exeunt
terms.comment: The reason given as the circumstance: “since, as”. Praesertim cum, all the more since. Quae cum ita sint, since this is so.
A reason both speakers know or can see.

evidence: Ter. And. 3.5.2: quandōquidem tam iners, tam nūllī cōnsilī sum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A stronger “since”, with a shade of “if that is how it is”.

phrases.latin: quī cum ūnā domō jam capī nōn possint, in aliās domōs tamquam in colōniās exeunt
phrases.english: since they can no longer fit in one house, they go out to other houses, as if to colonies

phrases.latin: cui Cossinius: quoniam satis bālāstī, inquit, ō Faustule noster
phrases.english: to whom Cossinius said: “since you have bleated enough, our dear Faustulus”

phrases.latin: dē pāvōnibus, inquit, līberē licet dīcās, quoniam discessit Fircellius
phrases.english: “you may speak freely about peacocks,” he said, “now that Fircellius has gone”

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
